chunks: Parts of a brushed motor, rotating vs static. The question: What are the parts of a motor? Which parts rotate and which parts remain static?
A brushed DC motor has two groups of parts. The static parts (the stator) stay still: the housing, the magnets, the brushes and the end caps.
The rotating parts (the rotor) turn: the shaft, the wire-wound core and the commutator. Knowing which is which explains how the motor works.
Picture a bicycle wheel with fixed brake pads touching the rim. The wheel (rotor) spins, and the pads (brushes) stay put and rub against it.
In the motor, the "rim" is a ring of copper segments called the commutator, and the pads carry electric current into it instead of slowing it down.
The analogy has a twist: the pads also help flip the current direction as the wheel turns.
Side cutaway of a small PM brushed motor. Blue/red: static magnets inside the steel can. Orange: everything that rotates (shaft, laminated core with windings, commutator).
Green: static brushes with springs pressing down on the rotating commutator, wired to the two terminals. Bearings carry the shaft; their outer races are fixed.
Stator: the stationary part: housing, magnets, brush holders. Rotor (armature): the rotating part: shaft, iron core and copper coils.
Commutator: a ring of copper segments on the shaft, each wired to a coil. Brush: a stationary contact, often carbon, pressed against the commutator.
Bearing: a part that lets the shaft turn smoothly in the housing.
Imagine one wire loop between two magnets. Its two ends connect to two half-ring copper segments. Two fixed brushes touch those segments.
Current flows in through one brush, around the loop, and out through the other, so the loop is pushed and starts to turn.
After half a turn, the segments swap places under the brushes, so the current in the loop reverses and the push keeps going the same way.
That is the whole idea: the brushes stay still and the commutator turns under them.
"A brushed DC motor has a stator that doesn't move: the housing, the permanent magnets or field windings, the end caps, the brush holders and the brushes.
The rotor, or armature, spins: the shaft, laminated iron core, copper windings and the commutator. Bearings let the shaft turn.
The brushes stay still and press on the rotating commutator to feed current into the windings and reverse it each half turn, so torque stays in one direction.
That sliding contact is also what wears out."
